read_prompt: Read the image file {path}. It is an enlarged crop of a few printed lines from one column of an 1854 Hebrew-English lexicon (Gesenius, Robinson translation). Transcribe every complete printed text line exactly, one array element per printed line, top to bottom. Preserve spelling, capitalisation, punctuation, printed abbreviations, section marks and end-of-line hyphenation. Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Syriac, Greek and Ethiopic must be Unicode text with every visible vowel point, dagesh, shin or sin dot, accent and diacritic, and with no point that is not printed; write them in logical order with no bidi control characters, keep the words of a right-to-left phrase in the order they are read, and keep the printed left-to-right order of separate items in a list. Transcribe the letters actually printed even when they are not the dictionary spelling: never insert or drop a vav or yod, and never replace a form with a more familiar one. Distinguish Arabic from Syriac by the letter shapes. If a line is only partially visible at the top or bottom edge, omit it entirely rather than guessing. Never add, reorder, translate, normalise or omit anything that is fully visible. If the crop contains no text, return an empty array.

lines.text: 3. God, the Mighty One, the Almighty.
In order to illustrate how far the Hebrew
usage in respect to the names of God, as
אֵל, אֱלֹהִים, יְהֹוָה, יָהּ, is synonymous,
we note here the following in respect to
this word: a) In prose, when spoken of
God κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν, it never stands alone,
lines.draft: God κατ' ἐξοχήν, it never stands alone,
lines.reread: God κατ’ ἐξοχήν, it never stands alone,
lines.note: The only difference is the mark after κατ. The print shows a raised Greek elision sign (koronis-shaped, curling like a comma above the baseline after τ), which in Unicode Greek is U+1FBD (᾽), not the ASCII apostrophe of Reading A nor the typographic right single quote U+2019 of Reading B. Everything else (italic God, ἐξοχήν with smooth breathing on ε and acute on η, the comma, and the English) matches both readings.

lines.text: but always either with an attribute, as
אֵל חַי, אֵל קַנָּא, אֵל שַׁדַּי, אֵל עֶלְיוֹן; or with
another name of God, as אֵל אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Gen. 33, 20; הָאֵל אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ Gen. 46, 3;
אֵל אֱלֹהִים יְהֹוָה Josh. 22, 22. Ps. 50, 1,
where it may be rendered, God of gods,
Jehovah, comp. Dan. 11, 36 אֵל אֵלִים; or
lastly with the genitive of a place or
person of which God is called the God,
as אֵל בֵּית־אֵל Gen. 31, 13. b) Far more
frequently it is the poetic name for God,
and stands in poetry very often alone,
sometimes with the art. הָאֵל, Ps. 18, 31.
33. 48. 68, 21. Job 8, 3. c) It takes the
suff. of 1 pers. אֵלִי my God! Ps. 18, 3.
22, 2. 11. The other suffixes are never
found with it; and for thy God, his God,
etc. is always said אֱלֹהֶיךָ, אֱלֹהָיו. d) It
is also a general name for a divinity, and
is thus used of idols; either alone Is. 44,
10. 15; or with an epithet, as אֵל אַחֵר an-
other god Ex. 34, 14, אֵל זָר a strange
god Ps. 81, 10.
To God is said in Scripture to belong
whatever is excellent, distinguished,
superior in its kind; since the ancients
were accustomed to refer all excellence
directly to the deity as its immediate
author. Hence אַרְזֵי אֵל Ps. 80, 11 cedars
of God, i. e. the loftiest, most beautiful,
as if planted by Jehovah; comp. עֲצֵי

lines.note: In both occurrences of the divine name the holem dot sits over the he (between yod and vav), with qamets under the vav, so the logical order is he+holem, vav+qamets (Reading B). Reading A wrongly stacks holem and qamets on the vav. All other characters, spacing, and the Ps./Gen. references agree in both readings and match the print.

lines.text: אל
lines.draft: אֵל
lines.reread: אל
lines.note: Line 1 is the large centred running head at the top of the column. It is printed without any vowel points: there is no tsere under the aleph, and no dagesh or other mark on the lamed. Reading A adds a tsere that is not on the page (the pointed אֵל appears only in line 2, "So אֵל הַרְרֵי"). Reading B matches the printed text exactly.

lines.text: So הַרְרֵי אֵל mountains of God Ps. 36, 7.
Comp. ἅλς δῖα, δῖα Λακεδαίμων. See in
אֱלֹהִים no. 6.
Plur. אֵלִים 1. mighty ones, heroes;
see above in Sing. no. 1.
2. gods, in a wider sense, spoken of
Jehovah and also heathen gods, Ex. 15,
11, comp. 18, 11. Dan. 11, 36 אֵל אֵלִים
God of gods, i. e. the supreme God. Also
בְּנֵי אֵלִים Ps. 29, 1. 89, 7, sons of the gods,
by an idiom of Heb. and Syriac syntax,
poet. for sons of God, i. e. angels.
Note. Following the example of most
etymologists, we have above referred אֵל
to the root אוּל; but to speak more accu-
rately, אֵל would seem rather to be a
primitive word, yet adapted in a certain
measure to an etymology from אוּל, so
that to the mind of the Hebrew it always
presented the idea of strength and power.
However this may be, we may note in
respect to Semitic usage: a) That from
the word אֵל (Arab. إِيلٌ, إِلٌ, and إِلٌّ)

lines.note: First Syriac word ends in a looped ܗ (he), not alaph (A) and with no yod or hbasa (B): it is the verb ܐܒܗ "to be a father". Two identical wedge-shaped zqapha marks sit above alaph and beth. The second word ܐܒܗܬܐ carries only syame over ܗ and no vowel points, so A's vowels and B's missing syame are both wrong.

lines.text: Among the Phenicians, ἬΛ, Ἴλος, was
lines.draft: Among the Phenicians, ἨΛ, Ἴλος, was
lines.reread: Among the Phenicians, ἬΛ, Ἴλος, was
lines.note: The capital eta carries two marks, identical to those over the iota of Ἴλος: a smooth breathing plus an acute accent. Reading A drops the accent (Ἠ), and Reading B makes the breathing rough (Ἤ). The printed letter is Ἤ (U+1F2C, psili + oxia), so the word is ἬΛ with capital lambda; everything else in both readings matches the print.

suff. אֵלַי, אֵלֶיךָ, אֵלָיו, אֵלֵינוּ, אֲלֵיכֶם,

lines.draft: אֲלֵיהֶם and אֲלֵהֶם, once אֱלֵיהֶם Ez. 31. 14,
lines.reread: אֲלֵיהֶם and אֲלֵהֶם, once אֲלֵיהֵם Ez. 31. 14,
lines.note: Decisive difference is the third word. Under its final he the print clearly shows three dots (segol), not two (tsere), so Reading B's הֵם is wrong. Under its aleph the pointing differs from the first word: the first word has a plain hataf patah (vertical shva plus patah bar), while the third word shows only dots with no patah bar, consistent with a partly faded hataf segol, which is also the attested Ez. 31:14 form. Everything else (yod present in words 1 and 3, absent in word 2; "Ez. 31. 14," punctuation) matches both readings.
